answer:
Key improvements, in priority order:

1. Fix internal inconsistencies that undermine credibility. (a) The summary says the company is 'registered' but later says no legal entity is formed. (b) It claims payments, deposits and verified accounts are handled in the app, yet the funding ask is to build in-app payments, damage protection and verified onboarding, so the pilot apparently ran without them. State clearly what exists today versus what is planned. (c) The pilot's 1,940 dollars at a 15 percent fee equals about 291 dollars, but 63 renters at 31 dollars average order implies roughly 62 orders, meaning most renters rented once or twice; reconcile the order count, the 44 percent repeat rate and the 3 to 4 rentals per year assumption, which the pilot does not support.

2. Rebuild the market sizing. The 2 to 3 billion dollar figure is a top-down assumption on purchase spending (19M students x 100-150 dollars), not rental revenue, and it is labeled 'addressable' when it is really total spend. The 5 percent capture and 50 million dollar volume claim also mixes spending with rental pricing (rentals cost about 70 percent less, so capturing 5 percent of spend is not the same as 5 percent of dollars). Recompute bottom-up: students per campus x share attending formals x rentals per year x average order x take rate, and show revenue (fees), not just transaction volume. Cite sources for 19M and 600 campuses. Note the survey is from one campus (n=412), so avoid generalizing nationally.

3. Add rigorous unit economics and a realistic revenue picture. Fee revenue of about 9,000 dollars in year one against a 25,000 dollar ask is thin; explain the path from there to a venture-scale or self-sustaining business. Address take-rate leakage (students can swap pickup in person and pay off-app), the hardest issue for peer-to-peer marketplaces. Include costs of payment processing (which eats a meaningful share of a 4.65 dollar fee), insurance, damage claims, customer support and ambassadors. Show CAC explicitly rather than assuming organic growth is nearly free, since the budget includes 9,000 dollars of marketing for four campuses.

4. Strengthen evidence on the core marketplace risks. Provide pilot data on lender supply versus renter demand (241 items but 63 renters means most inventory never transacted), listing-to-rental conversion, size and occasion availability, damage or non-return incidents, deposit disputes, and cleaning responsibilities. Explain how you will handle seasonality (long idle periods outside formal season) and retention beyond peak events.

5. Sharpen the competition and defensibility sections. Name actual competitors (e.g., Rent the Runway, Nuuly, Depop/Poshmark, campus Facebook groups, and any campus-specific rental startups) and compare on price, speed and trust. The moat argument (campus density, student org relationships) is plausible but unproven; show evidence such as org partnerships or lender concentration, and discuss how a competitor could replicate with a student-verification feature.

6. Be explicit about expansion and go-to-market. Explain how the second to fifth campuses will be seeded (chicken-and-egg supply problem), why ambassadors will work, the cost per campus launch, and the milestone that proves repeatability. A single-campus pilot of six weeks is a small basis for projecting 3,500 users and 1,400 renters; justify the multipliers or present base, low and high cases.

7. Address legal, safety and operational risk directly. Cover liability for damaged or hygiene-compromised items, deposits and payment compliance, university policies on commercial activity, age and identity verification, and insurance. This is currently deferred to the funding ask but is a core feasibility question.

8. Tighten the team and ask sections. All three founders are students with part-time availability; state commitment level, post-graduation plans for the seniors, and any advisors to fill gaps in operations and trust and safety. Tie the 25,000 dollar budget to measurable milestones and timelines (e.g., X campuses live, Y rentals, Z repeat rate by a given date), and clarify whether engineering funding pays founders or outside developers.

9. Presentation. Replace 'we think'/'we expect' claims with sourced data where possible, add a simple table of pilot metrics, a one-line value proposition at the top, and clear sections for traction versus projections. Remove repetition and keep claims proportionate to the evidence.
